An Introduction to Edward Said's Orientalism | A Macat Sociology Analysis | Cultures aren't wrong; they are different

The content of the video is all well and good, but I don't beleive the message is that cultures cannot be wrong. If anything can be wrong then why not a culture? Is a culture which encourages people to do wrong not also implicitly wrong?

Watch from 1:42 about the feelings the professor has regarding the partiers and the report he submits. this is Said's opinion now His argument is essentially just because a culture has values different than our own doesn't make those values wrong.

Generally speaking, no cultures encourage people to act wrong inside their culture. Whatever the act is might be labeled as wrong by the culture you originated in, but it's not labeled as wrong by the values of the culture the act originated in.

Shitty example

Joe was socialized in a culture that values never finishing the last sip of a beverage. Joe's friend Adam was socialized in a culture that values not wasting food and drink.

Is either friend's culture wrong for valuing what they do?

What you value as wrong or right can be totally different from what another culture values as right or wrong. This is because a culture can only be understood from the society it originates inside.

Joe's culture never finishes the drink because it's believed to give nourishment to dead ancestors. Adam's culture values food and drink because the older generations had very little during a long period of economic depression.

Both cultures are right, even though their values are different. Even better, neither friend/culture has to adopt the others values only accept them as valid.

edit: added the shitty example and split a paragraph to accommodate.

So I guess it is an argument for moral relativism. My initial impression was the core point was that we should be aware of our biases. I think the later is probably more universally accepted. Both points certainly have merit, but I can't help but intuit that there are some acts that are universally wrong regardless of the societal context.

Universally wrong regardless of the societal context.

That's something for /v/philosophy to grapple with. Although, I don't think the field has identified any universally applicable principles? If instance, the commonly proposed universal principles, "you should never take a life." This can be generally followed with, "what if your life is being threatened, what about killing animals for food, for sport, for entertainment, plants are alive too."

Philosophy cannot seem to answer any question (to my knowledge) with a universally applicable set of laws which hold in every situation, in all societies, at every point in time. This is the same across the social sciences, I think because society is so fluid and constantly changing. Compared to nature which is bound by a set of laws, understood to be constant across the universe and observed to be constant across time.
